I farm about 20 mu of flat alluvial ground here in Quzhou. My family has worked this land for generations, and I went through agricultural college, so I understand what I'm doing and why. The soil here is decent loam — good for grain — and the water table has been dropping every year, which I think about seriously.

I'm not going to experiment this year. The winter wheat–summer maize double-crop rotation is what this land does best, what the markets expect, and what I know how to execute well. Cotton income has collapsed and vegetables need more labor than I have. Two cash grain crops on the same 20 mu is the right call.

**For winter wheat**, I'll plant a local improved variety — something from the Hebei Academy of Agricultural Sciences, probably Shimai 22 or similar. It's not a hybrid but it's adapted to this soil and disease pressure. I'll do rotary tillage after the maize harvest to break up compaction and work in crop residue. I'll split my nitrogen — heavier base dressing at planting, lighter top-dress at jointing — because I've seen too many neighbors dump it all at once and watch it leach. Three irrigations: pre-sowing, overwintering, and grain-filling. I used to do four but I'm cutting one to protect the aquifer and frankly the yield penalty is small. Two pesticide passes: herbicide early and a fungicide/aphicide pass at heading.

**For summer maize**, I'll direct-seed a郑单958-type hybrid into the wheat stubble with no-till. The summer rains usually cover most of what the crop needs — I'll irrigate once if we hit a dry stretch in silking. Maize doesn't need much phosphorus and potassium from me at this point given the residual from wheat applications. One pesticide application targeting fall armyworm and corn borer if scouting shows it's warranted.
